content: In November 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) convened an expert consultation to review and discuss a preliminary draft of a document aimed at improving HIV program monitoring and management. This meeting included over 60 participants from various countries and partner organizations, such as program managers, healthcare providers, civil society representatives, and donors. The group validated a prioritization scheme of the top 40 indicators, with most existing indicators being modified to align with interim partner guidance and technical recommendations, rather than creating entirely new ones. The intended audience for this guideline includes HIV program staff and partners involved in collecting, analyzing, and using HIV-related strategic information at all levels of the health sector. This encompasses national-level staff responsible for developing policies, frameworks, and health information systems, as well as those working at subnational and service delivery levels. Other potential users include stakeholders such as non-governmental organizations (NGOs), private-sector care providers, civil society, and academic groups engaged in teaching and research. These stakeholders are encouraged to participate in government-led consultations to design or redesign strategic information systems in a transparent and accountable manner. The document is organized into three main parts. Part 1 outlines a consolidated framework for using strategic information to monitor and manage the health sector's response to the HIV epidemic, contextualized within the global strategy to end AIDS. Part 2 focuses on building strong strategic information systems for effective decision-making, including selecting and prioritizing country-specific indicator sets and adapting them to local contexts. It also highlights the components of a robust strategic information system. The guideline emphasizes the importance of strategic information for two primary objectives: program monitoring for accountability toward the 95–95–95 targets and Sustainable Development Goals, and program management through the analysis and use of disaggregated cascade data. The recommended indicators span the entire HIV results chain, focusing on outputs related to coverage and quality, as well as key programmatic and clinical outcomes. These indicators are designed to help managers adjust service delivery and improve quality and effectiveness. The HIV service cascade is a critical tool for visualizing the health sector's response to the epidemic, anchored by the 95–95–95 targets for 2030. The cascade format highlights gaps in service coverage and quality, enabling targeted interventions to improve patient follow-up and coordination between service areas. Routine cascade data reviews are essential for identifying gaps and tailoring responses to improve outcomes such as viral suppression. The guideline also promotes the use of individual-level data for patient-centered monitoring and case surveillance. As countries implement Treat All policies, individual-level data become increasingly important for ensuring high-quality services. Electronic medical records (EMRs) and unique identifiers can support person-centered care, facilitate case surveillance, and improve program management. However, these systems require stringent data security protocols to protect patient privacy and confidentiality. The delivery of HIV prevention, care, and treatment services depends on the strength of the underlying health system, which WHO defines through six building blocks: service delivery infrastructure, health workforce, medical products and technology, financing, health information systems, and leadership and governance. Monitoring these components is essential for effective HIV service delivery. Countries should routinely assess the adequacy of these building blocks and prioritize health system data in planning and resource allocation. Routine data reviews are a core function of program managers at all levels. These reviews should include a prioritized set of indicators analyzed at national, subnational, and facility levels. National program managers should conduct annual or more frequent reviews, while subnational and facility managers may review data quarterly or monthly to monitor progress and support efficient service delivery. Data dashboards can facilitate these reviews by providing standardized displays of analytic outputs, such as figures, tables, and maps, accessible to managers at different levels. In summary, this guideline provides a comprehensive framework for using strategic information to monitor and manage HIV programs effectively. It emphasizes the importance of routine data reviews, individual-level data systems, and robust health system components to improve service delivery, quality, and outcomes.
